en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 53.
The Training Rule on the Habit of Laughter.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of seventeen bhikkhus were playing in the water in the Aciravatī River.
At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had gone to the upper terrace of his excellent palace together with Queen Mallikā.
King Pasenadi of Kosala saw the group of seventeen bhikkhus playing in the water in the Aciravatī River.
Having seen them, he said this to Queen Mallikā:
“Mallikā, these arahants are playing in the water.
“Without a doubt, Great King, the Blessed One has not yet laid down a training rule.”
“Those monks are ungrateful.
Then it occurred to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“By what means might I not inform the Blessed One, yet the Blessed One would know that these monks have been playing in the water?”
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala had the group of seventeen bhikkhus summoned and gave them a large lump of sugar, saying,
“Venerable sirs, give this lump of sugar to the Blessed One.
Taking that lump of sugar, the group of seventeen bhikkhus approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala gives this lump of sugar to the Blessed One.
“But where did you see the king, monks?”

“Bhikkhus, you were playing in the water of the Aciravatī River,” the Blessed One said. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them: “… How can you, foolish men, play in the water? It is not, foolish men, for pleasing those who are not yet pleased…” [and so on]. I have laid down a training rule for bhikkhus: “Whatever bhikkhu should play in water, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is the training rule that was laid down. Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having been bitten by a snake, died from the bite of a snake. They told this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow you, bhikkhus, to play with water when it is for the purpose of medicine. This is the training rule that was laid down. Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, being thirsty, drank water from a stream. He became ill. They told this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow you, bhikkhus, to drink water from a stream. This is the training rule that was laid down. Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, being thirsty, drank water from a pond. He became ill. They told this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow you, bhikkhus, to drink water from a pond. This is the training rule that was laid down. Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, being thirsty, drank water from a reflection of a spoon. He became ill. They told this matter to the Blessed One. “I allow you, bhikkhus
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘In water, for the purpose of playing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
In water that is "fit for play" means:
if one, with the intention of playing, submerges, emerges, or splashes about in water that reaches above the ankles, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is water fit for play and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is water that is prone to laughter and he is doubtful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is water that is prone to laughter and he perceives it as not being prone to laughter, there is an offense of expiation.
If he plays in water that does not reach below the ankle, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If one plays in water with a boat, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one strikes the water with a hand, a foot, a stick, or a clod of earth, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one plays with water, sour gruel, milk, buttermilk, dye, urine, or mud contained in a vessel, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is water that does not have the nature of laughter, and one perceives it as having the nature of laughter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is water that does not have the nature of laughter, and one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is water that does not have the nature of laughter, and one perceives it as not having the nature of laughter, there is no offense.
There is no offense if it is not with the intention of laughing; or if,
having entered the water for some purpose, one dives, emerges, or swims about.
One who is crossing over may sink, or emerge, or struggle;
this applies in times of misfortune or for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The third training rule concerning laughing is finished.
